session.assistantText:
I'll start by understanding the workspace and the tool.
I have the full picture: `src/cli.js` is 5 lines (a fixed 3M-iteration loop that prints elapsed ms), `test/run.test.js` is a placeholder, and there is no git repo. Before touching code, here is my plan.

**Goal.** Every run appends its duration to a local history file. The tool then prints the median of the last N runs and how many of those runs were slower than a threshold.

**Design sketch.**
- Data shape first: a `RunRecord { ts, ms }`, one JSON object per line (JSONL), appended to a history file. A `Stats { count, medianMs, slowCount, thresholdMs, window }` value carries the summary.
- New module `src/history.js` owns the file: append, read back, compute stats. Pure functions for `median(ms[])` and `countSlower(ms[], threshold)`.
- `src/cli.js` stays a thin shell: run workload, time it, append the record, print the run line and the stats.
- History path resolution at the CLI boundary: `--history <path>`, else `RUNTIMER_HISTORY`, else XDG data dir. `--last N` (default 10), `--threshold MS` (default 50). A `stats` subcommand prints the summary without recording a new run.
- The window for both numbers is the same last-N window, so "slow" means slow relative to the recent history you are also looking at.

Let me run the design exploration before I commit to that shape.
Now the parallel design exploration. Two runners, same brief, separate output dirs.
While those run, let me finish the grounding and prep the pieces that don't depend on the design choice.
Baseline measured: the workload loop takes ~21 ms, so timing resolution and default thresholds matter here. Waiting on the two design candidates.
Both candidates converged on the same shape, which is strong signal. Let me get an independent cross-judge before I pick the base.
While the judge runs, let me settle the open questions myself and record the decisions.
Both candidates converged on the same shape, and the judge picked candidate 1 as base. Let me record the resolved contradictions, then delegate the implementation.
Now delegating the implementation with the settled shape and success criteria.
The implementation is in place. Now I verify it myself against the real CLI, not the delegate's word.
The missing-file case printed only the message, but the code I read prints the stats block too. The delegate may still be editing. Let me check.
The delegate was still fixing that case. Let me wait for it to finish, then do a full clean verification.
Now I run my own full verification on the final state, independent of the delegate's report.
The tests actually catch broken math. Now a full end-to-end check on the real CLI, including the paths the delegate claimed.
Your goal was to record each run's duration into a local history file, then print the median of the last N runs plus how many of them were slower than a threshold. That is built and verified.

**What you get**

```
$ runtimer
run took 13ms (checksum 8999994)

$ runtimer stats
runs recorded: 1
window size: 1
median: 13ms
slower than 50ms: 0 (of last 1)
```

`--last N` (default 10) sets the window, `--threshold MS` (default 50) sets what counts as slow. `--history PATH` and `RUNTIMER_HISTORY` both point at the history file, and the flag wins. The default file is `~/.runtimer/history.jsonl`.

**The design I settled on.** Two independent candidates came back with the same core shape, which is why I trust it: one append-only JSONL file, one module that owns it, and a pure function for the math. The judge picked that base and I grafted two things onto it, the total-run-count and window-size printed separately so you can see how much history the window dropped, and the exit-code table that gives every error case a deliberate behavior.

**The decisions I made for you**, since you left them open:
- The median and the slow count cover the same last-N window. Two numbers about two different populations is harder to read than it is worth. If you wanted "how many runs ever were slower than X", pass a large `--last`.
- A run exactly at the threshold is not slow. The comparison is strictly greater.
- A failed history write exits 1 but still prints the timing line first, so a script checking exit codes notices the history broke while you still see the number you asked for.
- A missing history file is not an error. `runtimer stats` before your first run prints a sentence and exits 0.

**Proof it works.** `.audit/verify.sh` runs the real CLI and compares real output across 37 checks. All pass. The unit suite is 16 tests, all green. I also mutated `src/stats.js` three ways to confirm the tests can actually fail: rounding the even median broke 4 tests, changing `>` to `>=` broke 1, and slicing the wrong end of the window broke 2. The file is restored and the suite passes again.

**Two things to know.** The default threshold of 50 ms is a guess against a workload that takes about 13 ms on this machine, so it currently reads "roughly four times as slow as normal". Change it per invocation with `--threshold`. And the history file grows without bound; there is no rotation, so delete it when it bothers you.

**The next engineer who owns this code** inherits four modules with a strict import direction. `src/history.js` is the only module that touches the filesystem. `src/stats.js` never sees a path. If you add a `clear` command or a second consumer, put it in `history.js` so there is still exactly one writer. The reasoning is recorded in `.audit/decisions.tsv`, and both design candidates are still in `.arena/` if you want to see what was rejected and why.
